opus-5.5.text:
I'd say I place moderate confidence in it — more than many skeptics, but a lot less than people sometimes assume when they see a clean line on a log plot.

The thing I trust most is the observation that loss goes down smoothly and predictably as you scale compute, data, and parameters. That's been remarkably robust across many orders of magnitude, and I don't expect it to suddenly break. Where my confidence drops off is the translation step: going from "the loss will be X" to "the system will be able to do Y kind of cognitive work." That mapping is really poorly understood. We don't have a good theory of how much reduction in perplexity buys you in terms of, say, being able to run a research project for a month without supervision.

So the way I tend to think about it is in terms of a wide distribution over how much effective compute you need. You can try to anchor on things like the amount of computation the brain does, or the amount of computation evolution did, or just extrapolate from how fast capabilities have been improving on tasks we care about. Each of those anchors is shaky on its own, but they don't point to wildly different answers. They suggest that transformatively capable systems are plausibly within reach in the next decade or two, and that's not a fringe possibility.

Then there are a bunch of additional uncertainties layered on top. Will we keep getting algorithmic progress at the rate we have been? Will people be willing to keep spending exponentially more on training runs? Are there qualitative capabilities — long-horizon planning, reliable agency, learning efficiently on the job — that don't fall out of scale the way next-token prediction does, and require some new idea? I don't think any of those is likely to be a hard wall, but each one adds spread.

If you push me for numbers, I'd put something like a meaningful probability, maybe fifteen percent or so, on AI that can do most cognitive work humans do by around 2030, and somewhere around forty percent by the mid-2030s. I'd caution people against treating those as precise. The honest summary is that the trend lines make it hard to rule out very fast progress, and that alone should change how seriously we take preparation, even if you aren't sure the extrapolation holds.

r001.rationale: The response says the mapping from loss to cognitive ability is poorly understood, but does not clearly distinguish having sufficient capability from the practical work of turning that capability into automation.

r002.rationale: It describes uncertainty in translating scaling trends into capabilities, but still treats the trends as informative and gives timing estimates; it does not state that they provide no reliable basis for predicting automation timing.

r003.rationale: It describes a wide distribution and gives probabilities at 2030 and the mid-2030s, conveying timing spread across multiple coming years rather than a single predicted year.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say moderate confidence, and I want to be careful about what exactly I'm confident in.

The thing I trust most is the empirical regularity itself. Loss goes down predictably as you scale compute and data, and that's held across many orders of magnitude. If you'd asked me in 2018 whether that would keep holding, I'd have put real probability on it breaking, and it didn't. So I've updated toward taking the trend seriously.

Where I get much less confident is in the mapping from loss to capabilities that matter economically. The scaling laws tell you about perplexity on a text distribution. They don't directly tell you when a system can do a week of a software engineer's job, or run a research project end to end. Those downstream capabilities tend to appear in a lumpier way. Some emerge earlier than you'd expect, some later, and we don't have a clean theory connecting them to the smooth curve.

So my actual method is something like: use the scaling trends to bound how much effective compute we'll have, then use benchmark trends and qualitative judgment to guess what that compute buys you. Each of those steps has maybe a factor of a few uncertainty in time. Stacked together, you end up with a distribution that's pretty wide. I'd put meaningful probability on systems that can do most cognitive work within something like a decade, and meaningful probability that it takes substantially longer.

I'd also flag that the extrapolation itself depends on continued investment. The trend has held partly because people kept spending exponentially more. If that spending stops, because returns look bad or because of regulation, the trend stops too. So it's not a law of nature, it's a law conditional on a certain economic picture.

The honest summary is that I think the trends are the single best tool we have, and they're still a pretty crude tool. Anyone claiming to know the year to within a couple years is overclaiming. But anyone who dismisses the trends as meaningless is ignoring the most striking empirical fact in the field.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes language-model loss from economically useful capabilities, but does not discuss the practical work of turning those capabilities into automation.

r002.rationale: It calls the trends a “pretty crude tool,” says the mapping to economically useful capability is uncertain, and rejects precise timing; this communicates that scaling trends alone are not a reliable timing basis.

r003.rationale: It gives meaningful probability to automation within about a decade and to it taking substantially longer, describing a wide distribution rather than a single-year estimate.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling trends are a pretty significant piece of evidence, but I’d be much more confident predicting something like loss on a particular distribution than predicting when we can automate most cognitive work. There are several steps between those two claims, and we don’t understand all of them very well.

You can observe that models get better as you put in more compute, and that this improvement translates into a broader range of useful capabilities. That gives you some reason to expect the process to continue. But it’s harder to say how much improvement you need before a system can reliably do a job that takes a human a week, including noticing when it’s made a mistake and recovering from it.

So I would use extrapolation to inform a fairly broad distribution over timelines. I wouldn’t take a particular curve, draw a line to ‘human-level intelligence,’ and have a lot of confidence in the date where they intersect. The uncertainty is partly about whether the trend continues, but a lot of it is about what level of performance would actually be sufficient.

r001.rationale: It separates improving model capability from reliably doing a human job, including detecting and recovering from mistakes, and says several steps lie between them.

r002.rationale: It says confidence is much lower for predicting automation timelines than for predicting loss, and rejects drawing a confident date from an extrapolated curve.

r003.rationale: It mentions a broad distribution over timelines, but does not say that Paul Christiano’s distribution for transformative AI capabilities is spread across the coming years.

sol-6.1.text:
I put more confidence in the qualitative prediction that scaling will keep producing more capable systems than in a particular date when those systems can automate most cognitive work. Those are pretty different claims.

We have this relatively smooth trend in how well models predict text, but then we’re trying to translate that into something like, “Can this system do a job that takes a human a week?” That translation is much less well understood. A system can be very impressive on short tasks and still have trouble maintaining a coherent plan, noticing when it’s made a mistake, or recovering without someone helping it.

I think there’s a real possibility that those problems turn out to be fairly straightforward—that with more capable models and some additional training, you get systems that can do long, useful projects. But I wouldn’t treat that as something established by the scaling curves themselves.

So scaling trends are a significant part of why I take relatively short timelines seriously. They’re not a strong basis for saying it happens in a particular year. A lot of the uncertainty is about what capabilities you get at a given scale, rather than whether the underlying trend continues.

r001.rationale: The response separates scaling-related capability gains from the less-understood work of getting systems to handle long projects, including planning, error detection, recovery, and additional training.

r002.rationale: It says scaling trends are not a strong basis for predicting a particular year when systems can automate cognitive work.

r003.rationale: It rejects confidence in a particular year and says short timelines are plausible, but does not describe a probability distribution spread across the coming years.
